newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS-D.Telekom profits strong as rivals gather.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-D.Telekom profits strong as rivals gather.

text.p: Germany's Deutsche Telekom AG on Tuesday reported strong profits for 1996 and said earnings would more than double this year as the company girds for a full-scale assault on its home market by new competitors.

At its first results news conference since it launched Europe's largest ever share listing six months ago, Telekom set out to show that it was matching the ambitious forecasts made during months of road shows to woo investors.
While providing no comparative figure for the previous year, Telekom said group net profit was 1.8 billion marks ($1.1 billion) in 1996. Sales rose six percent to 63.1 billion marks.

Net profit was hit by a 2.5 billion mark one-off charge to pay for job cuts to the year 2000 and the whopping 700 million mark price tag for its huge share offering that put around 25 percent of the company's capital in public hands in November.
Telekom chairman Ron Sommer said he would defend Telekom's home market against new competitors and predicted its market share would not be eroded quickly.
"I expect the market development will remain moderate," he told the annual results news conference. "We will fight for every customer and we won't make it easy for our competitors."

Telekom's business got off to a bad start last year as revenues were hit sharply in the first quarter by a public relations flop when it revamped calling charges and a software glitch that over-charged some customers on New Year's Day.

Business picked up in the second half and sales continued to grow in the first quarter of 1997. Pre-tax profit soared over 140 percent to 2.2 billion marks from 900 million the year before. Group sales rose eight percent to 16.3 billion marks.

Finance chief Joachim Kroeske said the strong growth in pre-tax profit was exagerrated by the low level of the previous year. But he said he was confident that full-year pre-tax income would be more than four times its first-quarter result.
"Multiplied by four would be a negative view. That would be very negative," he said, declining to give a forecast.
Telekom aims to double dividends on 1997 results to 1.20 marks from 60 pfennigs for 1996.

Telekom shares slipped slightly as investors took profits on the share's recent rise. Shares closed bourse trade at 40.13 marks, down 1.06 marks as the broader market edged up, but some analysts thought shares would continue rising.
"I can see the shares moving in the direction of 45 marks," said Juergen Elfers, analyst with BHF Bank in Frankfurt.
Telekom has cut debt and reduced its workforce faster than expected, a development welcomed by analysts.

Because of Telekom's improved financial situation, Kroeske said it would probably not be necessary to issue a second tranche of shares next year, unless Telekom planned to make a large acquisition that would require additional capital.
Despite Sommer's optimism, Telekom is beginning to feel the effects of competition. Its share of the domestic market slipped to 84 percent last year from 86 percent in 1995.
Revenues from outgoing international calls plunged 18.6 percent last year as it lost business to rivals.

Mobile phone division Deutsche Telekom Mobil Net GmbH, in fierce competition with rival Mannesmann Mobilfunk GmbH, saw net profits drop 51.4 percent to 67 million marks as a result of sharp price cuts that hit profit margins.

The Internet has loomed as a new threat to phone companies like Telekom because it enables users to make long distance calls at cheap, local rates. Telekom has dismissed the service in the past but now appears to have embraced the Internet.
"If Internet telephony ever generates real business, then Deutsche Telekom ... will profit to an especially large degree from that business," said Sommer.

Telekom is also struggling to hone its Global One alliance with France Telecom and Sprint Corp into a profitable global competitor. Its Atlas venture with France Telecom, which includes results from Global One, made a loss of 510 million marks last year on turnover of just over one billion marks.

Telekom is more cautious about foreign investments. Sommer said Telekom would initially refrain from investing in Spain's alternative operator Retevision, but retained an option to join the consortium led by France Telecom.
"We would be interested in an investment in any part of the world if it fits our long-term strategy," said Sommer. "I am speaking of where Telekom should be positioned in the year 2010 or 2015."
